---
title: "Manifest-first / declarative metadata"
---

::: {.callout-note appearance="default" collapse="false"}
**Q:** What is "Manifest-first / declarative metadata" design pattern?
:::

## The core idea

**Describe a component's identity, capabilities, and requirements as *data* — separate from and readable *before* the code that implements it.**

The manifest is the contract. The implementation is an artifact the runtime fetches *later*, only if the manifest says it's needed.

```
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  MANIFEST  (declarative, cheap, safe)   │
        │  ───────────────────────────────────    │
        │  name, version, capabilities,           │
        │  dependencies, entry point, config      │
        └────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                         │  read + validate FIRST
                         ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  LOADER / RESOLVER                      │
        │  builds registry, resolves deps,        │
        │  decides what to activate               │
        └────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                         │  activate on demand
                         ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  IMPLEMENTATION (imperative, expensive) │
        │  the actual code, loaded lazily         │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

"Manifest-**first**" is the temporal claim: nothing executes until the description has been read and understood.

---

## Imperative vs. declarative registration

The pattern is best understood by what it replaces.

**Imperative (code-first):**

```python
# plugins/__init__.py — must EXECUTE to learn anything
from .pdf_export import PdfExporter
from .dicom_reader import DicomReader   # imports pydicom, numpy... 400ms

registry.register("pdf", PdfExporter)
registry.register("dicom", DicomReader)
```

To answer "what plugins exist?" you must import everything. Discovery cost = activation cost. Untrusted plugin = arbitrary code execution at scan time.

**Declarative (manifest-first):**

```yaml
# plugins/dicom_reader/plugin.yaml
name: dicom-reader
version: 1.2.0
provides: [reader]
formats: [".dcm", ".ima"]
requires: { pydicom: ">=2.4" }
entry: dicom_reader.main:DicomReader   # a STRING, not an import
```

```python
manifests = [yaml.safe_load(p.read_text())
             for p in Path("plugins").glob("*/plugin.yaml")]
# Now you know everything. Zero plugin code has run.

chosen = next(m for m in manifests if ".dcm" in m["formats"])
cls = import_string(chosen["entry"])   # activate ONLY this one
```

---

## The four properties that make it valuable

```
1. INSPECTABLE WITHOUT EXECUTING
   Enumerate, search, validate, permission-check, render docs,
   build a dependency graph — all without running a line.

2. LATE / LAZY BINDING
   Discovery is O(read a small file). Activation is deferred.
   1000 plugins ≈ 1000 tiny YAML reads, 1 actual import.

3. UNIFORM SHAPE → TOOLING
   Because it's data with a schema: linters, IDE autocomplete,
   registries, diff/review, codegen, marketplaces.

4. INVERSION OF CONTROL
   The component declares WHAT it is; the host decides WHEN
   and WHETHER to use it. Host owns the lifecycle.
```

Property 1 is the security story (Android's `AndroidManifest.xml` permissions, browser extension manifests). Property 2 is the performance story. Property 3 is why ecosystems grow around it.

---

## Where you've already met it

| System | Manifest | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| npm | `package.json` | `node_modules/**/*.js` |
| Rust | `Cargo.toml` | `src/**/*.rs` |
| R packages | `DESCRIPTION` / `NAMESPACE` | `R/*.R` |
| Quarto | `_quarto.yml` + doc YAML header | `.qmd` body |
| Kubernetes | Pod/Deployment YAML | container image |
| VS Code ext. | `package.json → contributes` | `extension.js` (lazy activated) |
| Claude Code Skills | `SKILL.md` frontmatter (`name`, `description`) | the SKILL.md body + scripts |
| MCP | tool JSON schemas | the server handler |

That last pair is worth dwelling on, since you author both. A skill's frontmatter is a manifest whose `description` field is the *routing key* — the host reads only the frontmatter of every installed skill, matches against the task, and reads the body only for the winner. This variant has a name: **progressive disclosure**.

```
   ALL skills          ~50 tokens each     always in context
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ name + description  (the manifest)   │  ← cheap, eager
   └──────────────────────────────────────┘
              │ match
              ▼
   ONE skill            ~2000 tokens       loaded on demand
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ SKILL.md body, references/, scripts/ │  ← expensive, lazy
   └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Which explains a rule you've probably felt: a bad `description` makes a *good* skill invisible. In manifest-first systems, **the manifest is the interface** — quality of the description dominates quality of the implementation, because the implementation is never reached otherwise.

---

## Trade-offs (the honest part)

**Manifest drift.** Two sources of truth that can disagree — the manifest says `entry: foo:Bar`, the code renamed `Bar` to `Baz`. Declarative systems fail *at load time with a confusing error* rather than at compile time. Mitigations: schema validation in CI, or generate one side from the other (decorators → manifest, or manifest → stub code).

**The YAML-becomes-a-programming-language trap.** Declarative formats start clean, then acquire conditionals, then loops, then variable interpolation, then templating (Helm), and you've built a bad language with no debugger.

```
   expressiveness needed
        │
        │                          ╭── Helm/CI-YAML hell
        │                    ╭─────╯
        │        ╭───────────╯
        │  ╭─────╯  ← the sweet spot: static facts only
        └──┴──────────────────────────────► time / feature creep
```
Rule of thumb: **if a field's value depends on runtime state, it does not belong in the manifest.** Put an escape hatch (a code entry point) instead of growing the schema.

**Versioning.** The manifest schema is a public API. Once third parties write manifests, you can't rename fields. Include a `schemaVersion` from day one.

**Indirection cost.** For a closed system with 3 components you control, a manifest layer is pure ceremony. Just import them.

---

## When to reach for it

```
USE IT when ≥2 hold:
  ✓ open set of components (plugins, third-party, user-authored)
  ✓ discovery must be cheaper than activation
  ✓ components are untrusted or need permission gating
  ✓ you want tooling / a registry / a marketplace
  ✓ non-programmers need to configure or author components

SKIP IT when:
  ✗ closed set, all in-repo, all yours
  ✗ every component is loaded on every run anyway
  ✗ the "config" is really logic in disguise
```
